source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science 18(4):513-549
finding: Founding paper. Studies Tetris players. Defines epistemic action as action done to uncover information that is hidden or hard to compute mentally. Pragmatic action moves the player closer to the goal. Shows a standard information-processing model cannot explain player data, and that rotations that look useless in fact improve performance.
numbers: Only the abstract (via Crossref record) was read; publisher PDF blocked (403). Detailed numbers below come from Kirsh 1995 and Kirsh 2010, which cite this paper.
quote: actions performed to uncover information that is hidden or hard to compute mentally
limits: Full text not opened by us. Tetris is a fast, small, closed task; one lab and one game.
agent_relevance: Gives the design rule: an action is justified by information gained, not only by progress. Our write/sketch/run steps should be judged by what they reveal, not by whether they move the answer.

source: Kirsh (1995) The intelligent use of space. Artificial Intelligence 73:31-68
finding: Tetris players rotate falling pieces in the world to save internal computation. There is a burst of rotations early after a piece appears. External rotation is much faster than imagined rotation. The author calls this offloading: steps are not removed, they are moved from the head to the world.
numbers: Burst of rotations about 800-1800 ms after the piece enters (also stated as 800-1000 ms). External rotation as fast as 150 ms (also 200 ms). Mental rotation of a tetrazoid 1000-1800 ms, i.e. five to ten times slower.
quote: players will physically manipulate forms to save themselves mental effort
limits: Numbers are Kirsh's summary of the Kirsh and Maglio work, not the raw data. Speed gain is for rotation only.
agent_relevance: Cheap external moves can beat internal simulation when the external step is fast and the result is read back by perception. For an LLM the analogue is running code or writing a table instead of simulating in text.

source: Kirsh (1995) The intelligent use of space (generate-and-test process model)
finding: Process model: internal modules can request motor output directly, and the changed world feeds back to them. The agent and the world form one tightly timed computing system, bound by timing. A physical rotation supplies the generator in a generate-and-test loop with exactly what it needs.
numbers: Figure 11 sketch: internal components are nudged forward by inputs caused by the agent's own actions, unlike standard cascade models.
quote: this is a version of just in time inventory control, only here, the inventory is informational
limits: Qualitative sketch, not a fitted model with parameters.
agent_relevance: Supports a loop in S3/S4: the generator asks the environment (interpreter) for the next view and reads it back. Timing matters: request the external change just when the next step needs it.

source: Kirsh (1995) The intelligent use of space (three classes of spatial use)
finding: Classifies how people use space: arrangements that simplify choice, arrangements that simplify perception, and spatial dynamics that simplify internal computation. Data come from videos of cooking, assembly and packing, supermarket and workshop observation, and Tetris experiments. Example: a cook lays sliced vegetables in rows so length encodes number, which is easier to judge than area.
numbers: Qualitative video data; no sample statistics in the passages read.
quote: estimation of length is easier and more reliable than estimation of area or volume
limits: Observational, small N; a classification, not tested predictions.
agent_relevance: Three-way split maps to agent moves: restructure the problem to cut choices, make state visible (tables), and offload steps to a tool.

source: Kirsh (1995) citing Chambers & Reisberg (1985) and Reisberg (1987): imagery versus drawing
finding: Subjects could not find the second reading of an ambiguous figure (duck/rabbit, Necker cube) in a mental image. After drawing the image, all of them could reinterpret the drawing. An external trace can be reread; an internal image arrives with its interpretation fixed.
numbers: No subject reconstrued their image; 100% reinterpreted their own drawings (as quoted by Kirsh from Reisberg 1987).
quote: 100% of the subjects were able to reinterpret their own drawings
limits: Second-hand report; the original papers were not opened. Later work disputes parts of the imagery result (not checked here).
agent_relevance: Strong reason to make the agent write out its representation and then reread it fresh (S2), rather than keep reasoning inside one running text where the first reading sticks.

source: Kirsh (2010) Thinking with external representations. AI & Society 25:441-454
finding: Lists ways external representations add power: change the cost structure of the inferential landscape; give a shareable object of thought; create persistent referents; allow re-representation; are a more natural form for structure; allow more explicit encoding; allow arbitrarily complex structure; lower the cost of controlling thought. Claims that saving memory and computation is only part of the story.
numbers: Conceptual essay. Worked cases: right-triangle median sketch, jigsaw rearrangement, Tetris, protein folding.
quote: the obvious explanation--external representations save internal memory and computation--is only part of the story
limits: Mostly argument and examples, few new measurements.
agent_relevance: A checklist of what a scratch artifact can do for the agent; helps decide which external step to add (persist, re-represent, or compute).

source: Kirsh (2010) Thinking with external representations. AI & Society 25:441-454 (Tetris cost-structure case)
finding: In Tetris, subjects can rotate the piece in the head or in the world. Physical rotation is a bit faster than mental rotation, so the cost of sometimes over-rotating is repaid by faster and less error-prone decisions from vision. Kirsh notes that cost alone does not explain every case.
numbers: Cites Kirsh and Maglio 1995 for the timing; no new numbers.
limits: This case is explained by cost structure alone; jigsaw and other cases need more.
agent_relevance: Where an external step is cheap and reliable, use it by default; where it is not, do not.

source: Kirsh (2010) Thinking with external representations. AI & Society 25:441-454 (persistence and complexity limit)
finding: Mental structures degrade as they grow. Kirsh compares this to swap-space thrashing in a computer: trying a move mentally can destroy the structure being held, so the thinker cycles without progress. A physical state stays stable at any complexity. With enough external record keeping, some puzzles can be solved physically that could not be solved in the head.
numbers: Qualitative argument; no measured threshold (example: assembling twenty jigsaw pieces mentally).
limits: No quantitative test of the swap-space analogy in the paper.
agent_relevance: Matches why long chains of text reasoning fail: state is rewritten at each step. Keep state in a stable external record (variable table, file, grid) and read it back, G2/S4.

source: Kirsh (2010) Thinking with external representations. AI & Society 25:441-454 (external models and consistency)
finding: A built physical model counts as an existence proof of consistency: parts that can be present together cannot contradict each other. External models also reveal consequences their author did not intend.
numbers: Argument; example figures only.
limits: Philosophical claim; strength depends on the model being faithful.
agent_relevance: Running code is an external model that cannot lie about its own output. This is the base of G3 and G10: judge by outputs, not by the model's account of them.

source: Ross & Vallee-Tourangeau (2021) Catch that word: interactivity, serendipity and verbal fluency in a word production task. Psychological Research 85:842-856
finding: Letter-tile word production. Condition (high interactivity, low, shuffle) did not change the average number of words. Time spent moving tiles did: the longer a participant interacted, the more words. Accidental arrangements sometimes offered words (serendipity).
numbers: N=40 (32 female), repeated measures, 5 min each. Words: high 18.35 (SD 8.48), shuffle 17.22 (SD 6.23), low 17.02 (SD 6.59); F(2,78)=1.94, p=.146, partial eta2=.048. Number of shuffles did not predict output (0 shuffles M=18.9; 1: 15.87; 2: 17.00; 3: 16.90). Behaviour-based analysis was significant.
limits: Headline aggregate effect not significant; behaviour effect is post hoc and exploratory. Benefit went to those who used the affordance.
agent_relevance: Giving the agent a tool is not enough; the benefit follows actual use. Check that tool calls happen and that results are read back.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov & Ardislamov (2025) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra. Front Psychol 16:1691864 (failed replication, Exp 1)
finding: Conceptual replication of the claim that moving physical matchsticks raises success on matchstick algebra (Weller et al. 2011). Experiment 1 found no benefit of the interactive condition. Success was high in both arms.
numbers: N=105 after exclusions (108 recruited). Interactive assembled sticks (N=54): A .91, B .87, C .59, D .67. Static sticks (N=51): A .94, B .80, C .59, D .69. Baseline accuracy about 86% in static sticks.
limits: University students, Roman-numeral screening; solvers moved the sticks little even when asked.
agent_relevance: Failed replication: the physical-interaction advantage is not robust and depends on problem type. Do not assume a scratch step always helps.

source: Spiridonov, Erofeeva, Klowait, Morozov & Ardislamov (2025) The modulating role of sources of difficulty in interactive matchstick algebra. Front Psychol 16:1691864 (Exp 2 and 3, VR)
finding: Experiment 2 added static paper and interactive pre-assembled sticks, plus reminders every 90 s to use hands. Experiment 3 used virtual reality. Only one cell, VR interactive sticks, showed a clear gain; other contrasts were uncertain. More movements did not predict success.
numbers: Exp 2 N=88 (about 20-24 per cell), Exp 3 N=73. Bayesian logistic regression: VR interactive sticks +0.67 log-odds, 95% CI [0.22, 1.15], about 92% accuracy (+6 points); other conditions CIs include zero (e.g. Exp 2 interactive sticks +0.17 [-0.27, 0.64]). Total movements -0.015 [-0.042, 0.014]. Problem B -1.59, C -2.95, D -1.93. Five minutes beat three (+0.27).
limits: Small cells; high baseline accuracy; authors say movement can hinder when it does not match task demands (it interfered with relaxing higher-level constraints and did not help chunk decomposition).
agent_relevance: A scratch action must match the difficulty source; random fiddling can hurt. Gate extra actions on a signal, as in G1.

source: Weller et al. (2011) interactivity effect on matchstick algebra, as described by Spiridonov et al. (2025)
finding: As described by the 2025 paper, this research programme reported that handling physical problem parts raised success on insight tasks, with the biggest gain on the harder problem types (B, C, D, not A). The 2025 authors say interactive condition and interactive solution were conflated in that study. Later studies cited as null or mixed: Chuderski 2020, Ross and Vallee-Tourangeau 2020, Spiridonov 2021, Wang and van Leeuwen 2022.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Second-hand summary; the original studies were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: gains depend on problem type and on whether people actually act. The tool helps where it removes the actual source of difficulty.

source: Croom, Zhou & Firestone (2023) Seeing and understanding epistemic actions. PNAS 120(49):e2303162120
finding: Observers can tell from shaking motion alone whether someone is trying to learn the number or the shape of objects in a box. Epistemic intent is readable from behaviour, even when the box contents are identical and even when the player gets the answer wrong.
numbers: Exp 1: 16 players, 100% correct; 100 observers 76.2% accuracy, d=2.12. Exp 2: 18 players, only 4/18 correct in both rounds; observers 65.9%, d=1.53; for players wrong in both rounds d=1.70. Exp 3: same contents (20 cubes), 18 players, 100 observers 63.69%, d=0.86. Exp 4: minimal instructions 63.72%, d=0.85. Exp 5: 75% named information seeking; 74% named number or shape; chi2(1,N=96)=16.23.
limits: Forced-choice discrimination in one box-shaking task; shows perception of epistemic action, not that it helps problem solving.
agent_relevance: Epistemic moves have a recognisable signature. A logger could label scratch actions as probes versus commits, supporting separate handling of test moves and answer moves in the trace.

source: Pezzulo, Donnarumma, Maisto & Stoianov (2019) Making the environment an informative place: epistemic policies and sensorimotor enrichment. Entropy 21(4):350
finding: Computational account in active inference. A policy is scored by expected free energy, the sum of extrinsic value (reaching preferred outcomes) and epistemic value (expected information gain about hidden states). Epistemic value dominates when uncertainty is high; once context is known, pragmatic value takes over. Tetris rotation is cited as an epistemic policy.
numbers: T-maze simulation: the agent switches from an epistemic policy to a pragmatic one (policy 8 to policy 5 at trial 18).
limits: Toy simulations; link to human data is by example, not fit.
agent_relevance: A rule we could code: probe while uncertainty about the state is high, commit when remaining information gain is near zero. A formal version of S4 test before S7 select.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models
finding: Training transformers to write intermediate steps in a scratchpad lets them do multi-step computation that they fail at when answering directly. This is the clearest machine analogue of epistemic action: writing steps changes what the model can compute.
numbers: Addition (trained on 1-8 digits): beyond a critical size, scratchpad models solve it, while no-scratchpad models fail even at the largest size tested. 9-10 digit out-of-distribution: no-scratchpad models fail completely; scratchpad accuracy rises with size. Polynomial evaluation: direct 8.8% few-shot, 31.8% fine-tuned; scratchpad 20.1% and 50.7%. Program tracing: direct 11% / 20% vs scratchpad 26.5% / 41.5% (few-shot, scoring variant). Models 2M to 137B parameters.
limits: 2021 models; explicit scratch format, trained or few-shot; not a general reasoning model.
agent_relevance: Supports S4: write the working, not only the answer. Gains are largest where many dependent steps are needed.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided Language Models
finding: Let the model write the reasoning as code and let a Python interpreter do the solving. Beats chain of thought across 13 tasks, and holds up when numbers are large. The interpreter does the step the model is bad at.
numbers: GSM8K: PAL (Codex) 72.0% greedy vs PaLM-540B chain of thought 56.9% (about +15 points); with 40 samples 80.4% vs Minerva-540B 78.5%. GSM-Hard (large numbers): direct drops from 19.7% to 5.0%, chain of thought from 65.6% to 20.1%, PAL stays 61.5% in text (61.2% in table). Colored Objects +8.8 points over chain of thought; Penguins +14.1; Date +11.4; Object Counting 96.7% vs chain of thought 73.0%. Average of 3 runs.
quote: offloads the solution step to a runtime such as a Python interpreter
limits: Codex-era models; gain is largest where arithmetic is the weak point. Needs a problem that can be written as a program.
agent_relevance: A direct test of offloading: the model decomposes, the tool computes. Keep one learning step for the model and make the rest checkable by code (S4).

source: Chen et al. (2023) Program of Thoughts Prompting: Disentangling Computation from Reasoning
finding: Same idea as PAL, tested on five math word problem sets and three financial QA sets. Gains over chain of thought are largest where large-number arithmetic is needed.
numbers: Average gain over chain of thought about 12% across all datasets. Few-shot greedy: more than 8 points on GSM8K, AQuA, TabMWP; about 4 on SVAMP; about 20 on FinQA and ConvFinQA; about 8 on TATQA.
limits: Mainly Codex; the per-model table was garbled in text extraction, so only stated summary figures are recorded.
agent_relevance: Independent replication of the PAL pattern on other datasets. Gains are biggest when the model would miscompute.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Game of 24: letting the model propose, write down and evaluate partial states in a search over thoughts solves far more than plain or chain-of-thought prompts. The written partial states are external, inspectable scratch.
numbers: GPT-4 success on Game of 24: IO prompt 7.3%, chain of thought 4.0%, CoT-SC k=100 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. IO best of 100 33%, CoT best of 100 49%.
limits: Costs many more calls than one pass; G12 says search pays only where the model has some foothold. Toy search task.
agent_relevance: Structured scratch with state evaluation beats unstructured text at higher token cost. Compare at equal tokens before adopting (G7).

source: Yao et al. (2022) ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
finding: Interleaving thought with actions that query the world (a Wikipedia API, a simulated household or shop) reduces hallucination and error propagation seen in pure chain of thought. Acting to look things up is the epistemic action; the observation then constrains the next thought.
numbers: ALFWorld best ReAct trial 71% vs best Act-only 45% and BUTLER 37%; worst ReAct trial 48% beats the best BUTLER. ReAct over Act: relative gain 33% to 90%, average 62%. Absolute gains over imitation/RL: +34% ALFWorld, +10% WebShop. Error analysis: hallucination is 56% of chain-of-thought failures vs 0% for ReAct; ReAct failures: reasoning error 47%, search result error 23%.
limits: Few-shot prompts on small benchmarks; empty or useless search results derail the reasoning (23% of ReAct failures).
agent_relevance: Observation is the point: revise from real returned output (G2). Add a rule for what to do when the lookup returns nothing.

source: Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
finding: A model fine-tuned in a self-supervised way to decide which API to call (calculator, Q&A, search, translation, calendar), with what arguments, and how to use the result. Zero-shot results improve on many tasks.
numbers: Abstract-level read: improved zero-shot performance across downstream tasks, often competitive with larger models; no headline number extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and first figure were read; per-task numbers were not recorded.
agent_relevance: Model-chosen tool calls exist but depend on training. In our scaffold the program decides when to call the tool (SCHEMA section 1).

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Solving challenging math word problems using GPT-4 Code Interpreter with code-based self-verification
finding: Limiting how often GPT-4 Code Interpreter may use code shows its success rests on writing and running code, reading the execution output, and fixing the solution when output looks wrong. Explicit code-based self-verification, with the verification state used to weight votes, raises MATH accuracy.
numbers: MATH zero-shot accuracy 53.9% to 84.3% with code-based self-verification plus verification-weighted majority voting (abstract).
limits: Abstract-level numbers; the high figure combines verification and voting, so not a clean single-factor effect.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2/G3: a code check that tests the answer by an independent route, with its result used by code in selection.

source: Li et al. (2023) Chain of Code: Reasoning with a Language Model-Augmented Code Emulator
finding: The model writes pseudocode; an interpreter runs what it can and the model emulates the rest, line by line. Extends code as scratch to semantic sub-tasks.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard: 84%, a gain of 12 points over chain of thought; stated to beat the average human rater overall and the best human raters on an algorithmic subset.
limits: Abstract-level numbers; the emulated lines are model judgement and can be wrong.
agent_relevance: A mixed scheme: use real execution where possible and flag the model-simulated lines as unchecked.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: A zero-shot prompt asking the model to visualize the state after each reasoning step (as text grids) improves spatial reasoning. It is a sketch-as-thinking test. The gain disappears on a ring task the model can turn into arithmetic.
numbers: GPT-4 route-planning completing rate: VoT 40.77 vs CoT 37.02, no-viz 37.17, GPT-4V CoT 33.36; success rate 14.72 vs 9.48 / 10.28 / 5.65; next-step prediction 55.28 vs 48.61 / 48.49 / 46.59. Visual tiling: VoT 63.94 vs 54.15 / 46.98 / 49.62. Natural-language navigation: VoT 59.00 vs CoT 54.00 vs no-viz 35.50 (p<0.16 vs CoT). Ring navigation: CoT 52.5% beats VoT 49.5% (200 items).
limits: Main table is GPT-4 only; model visualisations are often wrong and not verified. Weaker models gain less.
agent_relevance: A text sketch helps when the task is spatial and no shorter symbolic route exists. Use as an operator, not by default (G1, G11).

source: Hu et al. (2024) Visual Sketchpad: Sketching as a Visual Chain of Thought for Multimodal Language Models
finding: Gives a multimodal model a canvas and drawing/vision tools so it can draw and look at its own sketch. Gains on math and vision tasks, largest on geometry-like and flow problems.
numbers: Average gain 11.2% on math for GPT-4o (23.4% for GPT-4 Turbo); abstract gives 12.7% math and 8.6% vision average. Maximum flow: GPT-4o 66.3%, +41.3 points. V*Bench +14.3 points (80.3%); BLINK average +9.0 for GPT-4o and +6.6 for GPT-4 Turbo; relative depth +12.1 for GPT-4o vs +2.4 for GPT-4 Turbo. Game boards +3 to 10 points. GPT-4o used the segmentation module on 40% of items.
limits: Gains depend on tool quality and on how well the model reads its own sketch; most plan errors come from failures of the vision specialists.
agent_relevance: The strongest recent test of sketch as thinking. The model must be able to read the drawing; verify that before adding a sketch step.

source: Pfau, Merrill & Bowman (2024) Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
finding: Challenges the idea that written steps work by being meaningful. Transformers trained with filler tokens ('......') solve algorithmic tasks they fail on with immediate answers. Extra tokens can give compute independent of content.
numbers: Filler tokens reached perfect accuracy on the tasks tested while immediate answer had low accuracy (as stated). Commercial models (Claude 2, GPT-3.5) show no gain from filler on common QA and math benchmarks.
limits: Needs specific dense supervision to learn; not seen in off-the-shelf models. Shows compute, not meaning, as one cause.
agent_relevance: A competing explanation: part of a scratch benefit is extra compute, not epistemic content. Test any scratch step against a same-length filler baseline.

source: Li, Liu, Zhou & Ma (2024) Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
finding: Formal result: constant-depth transformers without CoT sit in a small circuit class; with T chain-of-thought steps they can solve anything computable by boolean circuits of size T. CoT gives the ability to do serial computation.
numbers: Theory: constant-bit precision constant-depth transformers limited to AC0 without CoT; with T CoT steps, any problem solved by circuits of size T. Empirical: CoT lifts accuracy on permutation composition, iterated squaring and circuit value, most for low-depth models.
limits: Expressiveness, not learnability; real models may not reach the bound.
agent_relevance: A formal reason that written intermediate steps are real computation. Rule: tasks with long serial dependencies need written steps; short parallel ones do not.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning. ICLR 2025
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models. CoT helps mainly on math and symbolic or logic tasks, little elsewhere. Splitting plan from execution shows most of CoT's gain is in execution, and a tool solver beats CoT for that step.
numbers: Mean CoT gain: symbolic +14.2, math +12.3, logic +6.9. Top three categories 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without; other categories 56.8 vs 56.1. On MMLU and MMLU Pro, as much as 95% of CoT gain comes from questions with an equals sign in question or output. Plan + Tool Solver beats CoT and Plan + CoT Solver in most settings.
limits: Prompt-based CoT; modern reasoning-trained models were not the main subject.
agent_relevance: Strongest numbers for our rule: write, sketch or run code only when the task needs execution or tracking. Skip scratch for knowledge and commonsense items (G11), and prefer the interpreter to the model for symbolic execution.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Imagine while Reasoning in Space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT)
finding: Extends VoT so a multimodal model generates image visualisations as part of its reasoning. It is competitive with text CoT and improves on the hardest cases where text CoT fails.
numbers: Abstract-level read only: competitive performance across tasks and improvements in the most challenging scenarios where CoT fails. No table figures extracted.
limits: Only the abstract was extracted; numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Evidence that generated images can serve as scratch in the hard tail; effect not quantified here.

source: Gou et al. (2023) ToRA: A Tool-Integrated Reasoning Agent for Mathematical Problem Solving
finding: Open models trained to interleave natural-language reasoning with program calls reach strong math scores.
numbers: Abstract-level: 13% to 19% absolute average gain over open-source models on 10 datasets; ToRA-7B 44.6% on MATH, 22 points above WizardMath-70B.
limits: Trained model, not a prompt scaffold; only the abstract was read.
agent_relevance: Interleaved reason-and-run is a stable pattern that works even in small models once trained.
